Multiple-response questions

Source: vignettes/articles/table-multiresponse.Rmd
table-multiresponse.Rmd
library(spicy)
library(tibble)

table_multiresponse() tabulates one “check all that apply” question. Each item of the question is an indicator column, chosen or not, and one respondent can choose several items. The function reads the columns as one question: one row per item, with the number and the percentage of respondents who chose it. A last row gives the number of respondents behind the percentages.

With by, it compares groups. Each item gets a chi-squared test, or Fisher’s exact test when an expected count is below 5. The question gets a global test of all its items together, valid although one respondent can choose several items.

sochealth, the simulated survey shipped with spicy, asks one such question: “Sources of health information used in the past 12 months (check all that apply)”. Its five items are logical columns, TRUE when the source was chosen and FALSE when it was not:

info <- sochealth[startsWith(names(sochealth), "info_")]
head(info, 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   info_doctor info_pharmacist info_internet info_family info_media
#>   <lgl>       <lgl>           <lgl>         <lgl>       <lgl>     
#> 1 TRUE        FALSE           TRUE          FALSE       FALSE     
#> 2 FALSE       FALSE           TRUE          FALSE       TRUE      
#> 3 FALSE       FALSE           TRUE          FALSE       FALSE     
#> 4 FALSE       FALSE           TRUE          FALSE       FALSE

The 36 respondents who skipped the question are missing on all five items, and a respondent who answered without choosing any source is FALSE on all five. sex serves as the grouping.

One question, several answers

A respondent can choose several sources, and most respondents do:

table(rowSums(info), useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>    0    1    2    3    4    5 <NA> 
#>   67  462  422  168   34   11   36

The 1164 respondents who answered made 2001 choices: 67 of them chose no source, and 635 chose two or more. The NA column counts the 36 who skipped the question.

A tempting shortcut stacks the choices into one variable, one row per choice, and tabulates it like any categorical variable:

stacked <- data.frame(
  sex = rep(sochealth$sex, times = 5),
  source = factor(rep(names(info), each = nrow(info)), levels = names(info)),
  chosen = unlist(info, use.names = FALSE)
)
stacked <- stacked[stacked$chosen %in% TRUE, ]
nrow(stacked)
#> [1] 2001
table_categorical(stacked, select = source, by = sex)
#> Categorical table by sex
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %   p   
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  source            │                                                       .053 
#>    info_doctor     │   377       34.9     344     37.3     721     36.0         
#>    info_pharmacist │   137       12.7     119     12.9     256     12.8         
#>    info_internet   │   268       24.8     255     27.7     523     26.1         
#>    info_family     │   219       20.3     141     15.3     360     18.0         
#>    info_media      │    78        7.2      63      6.8     141      7.0         
#> 
#>  Variable          │ Cramer's V 
#> ───────────────────┼────────────
#>  source            │    .07     
#>    info_doctor     │            
#>    info_pharmacist │            
#>    info_internet   │            
#>    info_family     │            
#>    info_media      │            
#> 
#> Note. Group comparison: Pearson chi-squared test.

That table misreads the question in three ways.

  1. Its base is the choices. It has 2001 rows for 1164 respondents, and its percentages are shares of choices. They sum to 100 in each group, although one respondent can count in five rows.
  2. The respondents who chose nothing are gone. The 67 respondents without a source left no row to stack.
  3. Its chi-squared test is not valid. The choices of one respondent are not independent observations. They violate “the assumption of independence among units required by all the usual tests of independence on contingency tables” (Loughin and Scherer, 1998, p. 631). The test also builds its expected counts on each group’s total of choices, where the question is about respondents (p. 632). In the simulations of Loughin and Scherer, it was “a horribly conservative procedure” (p. 636).

The third fault hides a real difference here. Women choose more sources on average:

tapply(rowSums(info), sochealth$sex, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
#>   Female     Male 
#> 1.801336 1.631858

A share of the stacked table divides by the choices of its group, and women make more of them, so their shares come out smaller. The doctor is 34.9% of women’s choices, against 37.3% of men’s, although a larger share of women chose one, 62.9% against 60.9%. Loughin and Scherer describe this case: “the units’ multiple responses mask real differences between the rows” (1998, p. 632). Family or friends make 20.3% of women’s choices, against 15.3% of men’s, a gap of five points. The share of respondents who chose them differs by almost twelve, 36.6% against 25.0%:

tbl <- table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex
)
tbl
#> Multiple responses by sex
#> 
#>  Variable        │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %    p   
#> ─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  info_doctor     │   377       62.9     344     60.9     721     61.9    1.000 
#>  info_pharmacist │   137       22.9     119     21.1     256     22.0    1.000 
#>  info_internet   │   268       44.7     255     45.1     523     44.9    1.000 
#>  info_family     │   219       36.6     141     25.0     360     30.9    <.001 
#>  info_media      │    78       13.0      63     11.2     141     12.1    1.000 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │   599                565             1164                   
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 67 with no item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question). Item p-values: Pearson chi-squared test of each item by group. P-values adjusted for 5 tests (Holm method). Overall group comparison: Rao-Scott second-order corrected chi-squared test of multiple marginal independence, χ²(4.61) = 18.78, p = .002.

Each percentage is now a share of the respondents of its group, and the Respondents row gives those bases. The note explains the percentages and names the tests. Its global test finds the difference the stacked table missed: p = .002, against .053. The rest of the article reads this table piece by piece.

A first table

Without by, the table describes the whole sample:

table_multiresponse(sochealth, select = starts_with("info_"))
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable          │   n       %    
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────
#>  info_doctor       │   721    61.9  
#>  info_pharmacist   │   256    22.0  
#>  info_internet     │   523    44.9  
#>  info_family       │   360    30.9  
#>  info_media        │   141    12.1  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents       │  1164          
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 67 with no item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question).

Four things to notice:

  1. One row per item. n counts the respondents who chose the item, and % is their share of the respondents of the base: the percentage of cases.
  2. The percentages sum to more than 100. Here they add up to 171.9 before rounding, the mean number of choices per respondent times 100 (Jann, 2005, p. 107).
  3. The Respondents row is the base, the number of respondents every percentage is computed on.
  4. The note says what the percentages sum to and which respondents form the base: the 67 with no item chosen are in it, and the 36 with no data for the question are not.

select takes tidyselect syntax, so select = info_doctor:info_media and the five names written in c() give the same table.

Factor items and counted

Logical columns, like these, and numeric columns coded 0 and 1 are read as they are. A factor, character, or labelled column needs counted, the value that marks a choice. The same items recoded as "Yes" and "No" factors show the case:

yes_no <- as.data.frame(lapply(
  info,
  function(x) factor(x, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
))
table_multiresponse(yes_no, select = everything(), counted = "Yes")
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable          │   n       %    
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────
#>  info_doctor       │   721    61.9  
#>  info_pharmacist   │   256    22.0  
#>  info_internet     │   523    44.9  
#>  info_family       │   360    30.9  
#>  info_media        │   141    12.1  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents       │  1164          
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 67 with no item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question).

counted applies to every selected column. Any other non-missing value counts as not chosen, and a missing value stays missing. A labelled column is chosen where its code or its value label equals counted. A value that matches nothing is an error, so a typo cannot produce a table of zeros:

table_multiresponse(yes_no, select = everything(), counted = "yes")
#> Error in `table_multiresponse()`:
#> ! `counted = "yes"` matches no value of the selected columns.
#> ℹ Values found: "Yes", "No".

Labels and order

The rows show the column names by default. labels = TRUE prints the label attribute of each column, and a named vector sets the wording you publish. sort takes the values of freq(): "-" ranks the items by decreasing total count, and items with the same count keep the order of select:

table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  labels = TRUE,
  sort = "-"
)
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable                              │   n       %    
#> ───────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────
#>  Doctor or other health professional   │   721    61.9  
#>  Internet, websites or apps            │   523    44.9  
#>  Family or friends                     │   360    30.9  
#>  Pharmacist                            │   256    22.0  
#>  Television, radio or newspapers       │   141    12.1  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents                           │  1164          
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 67 with no item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question).

"+" ranks the items by increasing count, and "name+" and "name-" sort them alphabetically on the labels shown. The default, sort = "", sorts nothing: the rows keep the order in which select delivers the columns, their order in the data with starts_with() or info_doctor:info_media, or the order written in c(). The function cannot know the questionnaire, so its order comes from the order of the columns or the order written in select.

Bases and percentages

The base is the set of respondents a percentage of cases is computed on. Three bases are in use, and they differ on two kinds of respondents: those who chose nothing and those who skipped the question. sochealth has both: 67 respondents chose no source, and 36 skipped the question.

The default, base = "valid", keeps every respondent with at least one non-missing item. It is the base of the first table: the 67 stay, the 36 leave, and the note gives both counts. Within the base, a missing item counts as not chosen, which matters when a respondent skips some items and answers others. This is how expss counts its valid cases. It is also the base of Stata’s mrtab with its include option (Jann, 2005, p. 99). Jann uses that option in his own example, because its list of income types “is probably not exhaustive” (pp. 107-108).

base = "answered" keeps only the respondents who chose at least one item:

table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  base = "answered"
)
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable          │   n       %    
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────
#>  info_doctor       │   721    65.7  
#>  info_pharmacist   │   256    23.3  
#>  info_internet     │   523    47.7  
#>  info_family       │   360    32.8  
#>  info_media        │   141    12.9  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents       │  1097          
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with at least one item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question and 67 with no item chosen).

This is the default of SPSS MULT RESPONSE and of mrtab (Jann, 2005, p. 98). Under this base, choosing nothing cannot be told from skipping, so the 67 respondents who chose no source leave with the 36 who skipped. The note counts the two groups apart, and every percentage rises: 65.7% chose a doctor, against 61.9% under "valid". Jann states the dilemma: “it is often not clear a priori whether the respondent refused to answer the question (and thus should be excluded from analysis) or whether the correct response is simply ‘none’” (p. 107).

base = "all" keeps every row, as questionr::multi.table() does:

table_multiresponse(sochealth, select = starts_with("info_"), base = "all")
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable          │   n       %    
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────
#>  info_doctor       │   721    60.1  
#>  info_pharmacist   │   256    21.3  
#>  info_internet     │   523    43.6  
#>  info_family       │   360    30.0  
#>  info_media        │   141    11.8  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents       │  1200          
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: all respondents, including 36 with no data for the question and 67 with no item chosen.

The 36 respondents who skipped the question now enter the base, and every percentage counts them as choosing nothing. The note still keeps them apart from the 67 who chose no source: the base includes 36 with no data for the question and 67 with no item chosen.

The counts are the same under the three bases. The percentages and the tests are not. "valid" assumes that a skipped question is coded missing on every item, and that a box left unchecked is coded FALSE or 0, as in sochealth. In data that code an unchecked box as missing, "valid" would drop the respondents who checked nothing. "all" keeps them, along with those who skipped the question.

Percentages of cases or of responses

percent sets what a percentage is of. "cases", the default, divides by the respondents of the base. "responses" divides by all the choices made in the group, so the column sums to 100. "both" shows the two:

table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  percent = "both"
)
#> Multiple responses
#> 
#>  Variable          │   n      % of cases    % of responses  
#> ───────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────
#>  info_doctor       │   721       61.9            36.0       
#>  info_pharmacist   │   256       22.0            12.8       
#>  info_internet     │   523       44.9            26.1       
#>  info_family       │   360       30.9            18.0       
#>  info_media        │   141       12.1             7.0       
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents       │  1164                                  
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages of cases can sum to more than 100%, and percentages of responses sum to 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 67 with no item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question).

The percentages of responses are the shares of the stacked table, and the note now describes both columns. The percentages of cases stay the default for three reasons. The papers on these tests tabulate them (Agresti and Liu, 1999, p. 937; Bilder and Loughin, 2004, p. 242). Jann finds that “usually, it is proportions on the basis of observations one is interested in” (2005, p. 98). And they are what the tests compare: for each item, the probability that a respondent of each group chooses it.

Comparing groups

tbl, the table of the first section, compares women and men. With by, the counts and percentages are given for each group and for the Total margin. Rows with a missing by are removed, and the note says how many. The tests come in two layers: one per item, and one for the question.

One test per item

Each item gets the Pearson chi-squared test of its table of groups by chosen or not, on r − 1 degrees of freedom for r groups. The arithmetic is that of chisq.test(correct = FALSE): no continuity correction, and no constant added to an empty cell (Agresti and Liu, 1999).

When an expected count of an item’s table is below 5, the chi-squared approximation is unreliable, and the item takes Fisher’s exact test instead. This is the rule of test = "auto", the default, shared with table_categorical() and gtsummary’s add_p(). In tbl, every expected count is far above 5. A smaller sample split into more groups is another matter: in the South region, 31 respondents aged 65 to 75 answered the question, and the media item has an expected count of 3.2 among them:

table_multiresponse(
  subset(sochealth, region == "South"),
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = age_group
)
#> Multiple responses by age_group
#> 
#>  Variable        │ 25-34 n  25-34 %  35-49 n  35-49 %  50-64 n  50-64 % 
#> ─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  info_doctor     │   27      57.4      36      52.2      33      67.3   
#>  info_pharmacist │    8      17.0      17      24.6      12      24.5   
#>  info_internet   │   35      74.5      39      56.5      19      38.8   
#>  info_family     │   17      36.2      21      30.4      15      30.6   
#>  info_media      │    3       6.4       6       8.7       4       8.2   
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │   47                69                49             
#> 
#>  Variable        │ 65-75 n  65-75 %  Total n  Total %    p   
#> ─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────
#>  info_doctor     │   22      71.0      118     60.2     .624 
#>  info_pharmacist │    9      29.0       46     23.5    1.000 
#>  info_internet   │    3       9.7       96     49.0    <.001 
#>  info_family     │   10      32.3       63     32.1    1.000 
#>  info_media      │    7      22.6       20     10.2     .591 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │   31                196                   
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 10 with no item chosen (excluded: 5 with no data for the question). Item p-values: Pearson chi-squared test (info_doctor, info_pharmacist, info_internet, info_family); Fisher exact test (info_media). P-values adjusted for 5 tests (Holm method). Overall group comparison: Rao-Scott second-order corrected chi-squared test of multiple marginal independence, χ²(13.78) = 44.16, p < .001.

The note names both tests: the Pearson chi-squared for four items, and Fisher’s exact test for info_media, which has no statistic. test = "chisq" and test = "fisher" take one test for every item. With two groups, as in tbl, each item’s table is 2x2, and test = "midp" and test = "n1" take the Fisher mid-p test and Campbell’s N-1 chi-squared test, presented in Categorical summary tables.

Back in tbl, every item takes the chi-squared. The data frame output keeps the test, the statistics and both p-values:

wide <- table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex,
  output = "data.frame"
)
wide[c("Variable", "test_type", "Chi2", "df", "p", "p_unadjusted")]
#>          Variable   test_type        Chi2 df            p p_unadjusted
#> 1     info_doctor chi_squared  0.51997605  1 1.000000e+00 4.708519e-01
#> 2 info_pharmacist chi_squared  0.55490963  1 1.000000e+00 4.563185e-01
#> 3   info_internet chi_squared  0.01801149  1 1.000000e+00 8.932390e-01
#> 4     info_family chi_squared 18.33047265  1 9.285636e-05 1.857127e-05
#> 5      info_media chi_squared  0.95631714  1 1.000000e+00 3.281165e-01
#> 6     Respondents        <NA>          NA NA           NA           NA

The p column is adjusted by Holm’s method, and p_unadjusted keeps the raw values. The items of one question form a natural family of tests, read together, so the adjustment is on by default. table_categorical() defaults to "none", because there each test belongs to a different variable.

The papers that test the items one by one adjust them by Bonferroni (Agresti and Liu, 1999, p. 941). Holm’s method controls the same family-wise error rate, whatever the dependence between the items. R’s documentation sees “no reason to use the unmodified Bonferroni correction because it is dominated by Holm’s method” (?p.adjust). Holm’s smallest adjusted p-value, that of family, is five times the smallest raw p-value: the Bonferroni global p-value of Agresti and Liu (1999).

The note names the method and the number of items adjusted together. p_adjust = "none" keeps the raw p-values, and another method of stats::p.adjust() can be named instead. statistic = TRUE prints the statistics in a Test column, χ²(1) = 18.33 for family, with or without the p-values. An item tested exactly shows a dash there.

One test for the question

Agresti and Liu read the item tests as a follow-up: “When this overall test gives evidence against the null hypothesis, the separate chi-squared components provide information about the marginal tables that are responsible” (1999, p. 941). The overall test is the last sentence of the note. It tests multiple marginal independence: that the probability of choosing each item is the same in every group.

Its statistic is the sum of the item chi-squared statistics, 20.38 here, whatever test the item p-values take. The sum does not depend on which answer of an item is coded as chosen (Agresti and Liu, 1999). It is not chi-squared under the null hypothesis: one respondent can choose several items, so the items are correlated (Loughin and Scherer, 1998). Its asymptotic distribution is a weighted sum of chi-squared variables, the weights being the eigenvalues of a design-effect matrix (Bilder, Loughin and Nettleton, 2000, Appendix A).

The mean of those weights is 1, but “individual weights may differ from one” (Thomas and Decady, 2004, p. 48). The default, global_test = "rs2", allows for their spread with the second-order Rao-Scott correction of Thomas and Decady (2004, pp. 48 and 58-59). It matches the first two moments of the distribution and refers the result to a chi-squared on fractional degrees of freedom: χ²(4.61) = 18.78 here. The result is deterministic.

glance() returns the global test as numbers:

broom::glance(tbl)[c("test_type", "statistic", "df", "p.value", "rs_cv")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   test_type statistic    df p.value rs_cv
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 rs2            18.8  4.61 0.00151 0.291

rs_cv measures the spread of those weights: their coefficient of variation, their mean being taken as 1. It estimates the coefficient a of Thomas and Decady (2004, pp. 48 and 59). The correction divides the sum by 1 + rs_cv² and refers it to a chi-squared on c(r − 1)/(1 + rs_cv²) degrees of freedom, for c items and r groups (p. 48). Here 1 + 0.29² = 1.08, so 20.38 on 5 degrees of freedom becomes 18.78 on 4.61. The closer rs_cv is to 0, the less the correction changes. Thomas and Decady read this coefficient to decide whether the second order is needed (pp. 53 and 57).

The bootstrap

global_test = "bootstrap" refers the same sum to its distribution over boot_n resamples, 1999 by default. Each resample draws whole response vectors with replacement from the pooled respondents, with the group sizes held fixed (Loughin and Scherer, 1998). The p-value is the share of resamples whose sum is at least the observed one. It is random, so set a seed to reproduce it:

set.seed(1)
boot <- table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex,
  global_test = "bootstrap"
)
broom::glance(boot)[c("test_type", "statistic", "df", "p.value", "boot_n")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   test_type statistic    df p.value boot_n
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>  <int>
#> 1 bootstrap      20.4    NA 0.00150   1999

The statistic is the uncorrected sum, 20.38, with no degrees of freedom. Three of the 1999 resamples reached it, so the p-value is 3/1999, printed as p = .002 in the note. A p-value of 0 would only say that no resample reached the sum. The note then reports it as below one resample in boot_n, rounded up.

A resample in which an item is chosen by every respondent or by none gives that item no statistic. It is drawn again, as Bilder, Loughin and Nettleton (2000, p. 1298) do, and attr(boot, "global_test")$boot_redraws counts the redraws. The bootstrap held its level in most published settings, with exceptions that Bilder, Loughin and Nettleton report (2000, p. 1305). No study of multiple marginal independence compares it with the second-order test.

Items nobody chose

An item chosen by every respondent, or by none, has no test, but its row stays. A sixth source that nobody chose is added here on purpose, missing like the others for the respondents who skipped the question:

with_empty <- transform(
  sochealth,
  info_other = ifelse(is.na(info_doctor), NA, FALSE)
)
table_multiresponse(with_empty, select = starts_with("info_"), by = sex)
#> Multiple responses by sex
#> 
#>  Variable        │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total %    p   
#> ─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  info_doctor     │   377       62.9     344     60.9     721     61.9    1.000 
#>  info_pharmacist │   137       22.9     119     21.1     256     22.0    1.000 
#>  info_internet   │   268       44.7     255     45.1     523     44.9    1.000 
#>  info_family     │   219       36.6     141     25.0     360     30.9    <.001 
#>  info_media      │    78       13.0      63     11.2     141     12.1    1.000 
#>  info_other      │     0        0.0       0      0.0       0      0.0     –    
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │   599                565             1164                   
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 67 with no item chosen (excluded: 36 with no data for the question). Item p-values: Pearson chi-squared test of each item by group. P-values adjusted for 5 tests (Holm method). Not tested (no variation, shown as –): info_other. Overall group comparison: Rao-Scott second-order corrected chi-squared test of multiple marginal independence, χ²(4.61) = 18.78, p = .002.

Its row shows a true zero and its p cell a dash, which the note explains. The item leaves the global test, which is unchanged, and the Holm adjustment, which still counts five tests. With fewer than two groups holding respondents, there is nothing to compare, and the table shows no test.

Descriptive tables

Some reports describe without testing. STROBE advises that “significance tests should be avoided in descriptive tables” (Vandenbroucke et al., 2007, p. 1643). A report on a small survey that reached nearly all of its population, for instance, may show no test at all.

p_value = FALSE removes the p column and the global test from every output, the data frames included. The first 80 respondents stand in for such a small survey:

small <- head(sochealth, 80)
table_multiresponse(
  small,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex,
  p_value = FALSE,
  percent_digits = 0
)
#> Multiple responses by sex
#> 
#>  Variable        │ Female n  Female %  Male n  Male %  Total n  Total % 
#> ─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  info_doctor     │    21        52       19      49      40       51    
#>  info_pharmacist │    11        28        8      21      19       24    
#>  info_internet   │    19        48       25      64      44       56    
#>  info_family     │    11        28        5      13      16       20    
#>  info_media      │     5        12        5      13      10       13    
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  Respondents     │    40                 39              79             
#> 
#> Note. Multiple answers possible: percentages can sum to more than 100%. Base: respondents with data for the question, including 7 with no item chosen (excluded: 1 with no data for the question).

statistic stays independent of p_value, so statistic = TRUE would still show each item’s chi-squared. A p_adjust typed with p_value = FALSE is an error, since there is nothing to adjust.

percent_digits = 0 follows the AMA manual: “A percentage or decimal quotient should contain no more than the number of digits in the denominator” (American Medical Association, 2020, section 4.1.8). Groups of fewer than 100 respondents, 40 and 39 here, therefore take whole percentages.

The note answers two more rules. The AMA manual asks that “any discrepancy in the sum of percentages in a tabulation” be explained, and it names “multiple procedures” among the causes (section 18.7.2). JAMA’s instructions for tables ask authors to “explain any empty cells”. They also ask to “add a footnote to explain why numbers may not sum to group totals or percentages do not add to 100%” (JAMA Network, 2016, p. 2). The note says why the percentages of cases exceed 100, and what the dash of an untested item means. The Respondents row gives the denominator once for all the items, as the AMA manual allows for “a series of proportions or percentages drawn from the same sample” (section 18.7.3).

Citing a cell in running text

inline() returns one cell as the table prints it, so a number quoted in a sentence cannot drift from the table. An item is addressed by its column name. The groups are spanners, so model selects one, the Total margin included:

inline(tbl, info_family, column = "pct", model = "Female")
#> [1] "36.6"
inline(tbl, info_family, column = "{n} ({pct}%)", model = "Male")
#> [1] "141 (25.0%)"

The item p belongs to no group and is cited without model. The Respondents row is the fit statistic "nobs":

inline(tbl, info_family, column = "p")
#> [1] "<.001"
inline(tbl, "nobs", model = "Female")
#> [1] "599"

The statistic needs a table built with statistic = TRUE:

tbl_stat <- table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex,
  statistic = TRUE
)
inline(tbl_stat, info_family, column = "statistic")
#> [1] "χ²(1) = 18.33"

Without column, inline() returns the count. In a grouped table it still needs model, and its error lists the groups. The global test has no cell: it lives in the note and in glance().

Downstream: the raw frame and the broom views

output = "data.frame" returns the wide frame at full precision: one row per item, a last row with the base, and columns named after the groups:

names(wide)
#>  [1] "Variable"     "Female n"     "Female %"     "Male n"       "Male %"      
#>  [6] "Total n"      "Total %"      "test_type"    "Chi2"         "df"          
#> [11] "p"            "p_unadjusted"

output = "long" returns one row per item and group, with the base of the group:

long <- table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex,
  output = "long"
)
head(long, 3)
#>      variable  group   n base      pct   test_type      chi2 df p p_unadjusted
#> 1 info_doctor Female 377  599 62.93823 chi_squared 0.5199761  1 1    0.4708519
#> 2 info_doctor   Male 344  565 60.88496 chi_squared 0.5199761  1 1    0.4708519
#> 3 info_doctor  Total 721 1164 61.94158 chi_squared 0.5199761  1 1    0.4708519

Both frames carry the note in attr(x, "note") and the global test in attr(x, "global_test").

tidy() returns one row per item and group, the margin flagged by total, with the proportions of respondents and of responses. glance() returns one row for the question:

broom::tidy(tbl)
#> # A tibble: 15 × 13

broom::glance(tbl)

Both column sets are fixed: a column the table does not show, such as boot_n under the Rao-Scott test, is present and NA. Index by name, never by position.

Comparison with other tools

Each tool settles the same four points in its own way: what a percentage is of, an item nobody chose, a respondent who did not answer, and the tests.

  • SPSS MULT RESPONSE computes percentages on cases by default (BASE = CASES), and its cross-tabulations show counts unless CELLS asks for percentages. An item nobody chose does not appear. Under the default MISSING = TABLE, a respondent who chose no item of a dichotomy group is missing, as under base = "answered". It offers no test.
  • Stata mrtab prints percentages of responses and of cases in its one-way table, and either one in a two-way table. It keeps the respondents with at least one response by default, include gives base = "valid", and includemissing gives base = "all" (Jann, 2005, pp. 98-99). Its overall Pearson test on the response patterns is “only suited if there are very few categories” (p. 115). mtest() tests each item, adjusted by bonferroni, holm or sidak, or not.
  • expss divides by the valid cases, those with at least one non-missing value (cross_cpct()), or by the responses (cross_cpct_responses()). Its column tests (significance_cpct()) are z tests, without Bonferroni adjustment by default.
  • questionr divides by every row in multi.table(), rows with all items missing included, and counts a missing item as not chosen. cross.multi.table() divides by the size of the group. An item nobody chose shows 0. It offers no test.
  • gtsummary, with type = "dichotomous", gives n (%) of the non-missing answers of each item, with an “Unknown” row for its missing values. A 0/1 item that nobody chose is an error unless it is a factor with a level 1. add_p() tests each item by a chi-squared test without continuity correction, or by Fisher’s exact test when an expected count is below 5. It adjusts nothing and has no global test.
  • MRCV gives counts, not percentages, and does not handle missing values. Its global tests are the bootstrap, the second-order Rao-Scott correction, and Bonferroni, all three by default. If an item lacks a 0 or a 1, every global test is NA. It adds 0.5 to the empty cells before each item statistic. table_multiresponse() reproduces its Rao-Scott test on the Kansas farmer data of Loughin and Scherer (1998), pinned in the package tests.

table_multiresponse() makes its four choices explicit: percentages of cases, the "valid" base with both counts in the note, items nobody chose kept at zero, and Holm-adjusted item tests with a Rao-Scott global test.

Output engines

The same table renders through six further engines, the console being the reference.

table_multiresponse(sochealth, select = starts_with("info_"), output = "gt")
table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  output = "tinytable"
)
table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  output = "flextable"
)
table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  output = "excel",
  excel_path = "info_sources.xlsx"
)
table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  output = "word",
  word_path = "info_sources.docx"
)
table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  output = "clipboard"
)

A journal style moves the defaults of the whole table, as elsewhere in the family. Under style = "jama", p-values take two decimals, and three below .01:

table_multiresponse(
  sochealth,
  select = starts_with("info_"),
  by = sex,
  style = "jama"
)
#> Multiple responses by sex
